channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Water
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] Russia-aligned hacktivists have tampered with exposed water and industrial controls since 2024, Bloomberg reports; Denmark officially blamed Z-Pentest for a waterworks attack that burst pipes
item.category: Top Story
item.description: Bloomberg News published a review on 27 October of a loose network of Russia-sympathetic hackers that it says has carried out hundreds of attacks since 2024 on water treatment plants, factories, dams and similar sites in countries seen as hostile to Russia. The best-documented water case is the December 2024 attack on Tureby Alkestrup Waterworks in Køge, Denmark: Bloomberg reports that the pressure-control system was reset to zero, that pressure surged on restart and burst underground pipes, that the pump maker found the system had been hacked, and that its password was “1234”. Denmark’s Defence Intelligence Service attributed the attack to Z-Pentest in December 2025 and says the group has links to the Russian state; Danish authorities put the impact at about 50 households without water for seven hours and 450 homes for one hour, while Bloomberg reports that 450 homes lost water. Bloomberg also reports that control settings were changed at an unnamed Texas public water system in 2024, spilling water from its reservoirs, and describes cases outside water, including a Los Angeles-area meatpacker whose refrigeration was shut off before an ammonia leak, and incidents in Spain at a crematorium, a transformer factory and two wineries. Who confirmed each case is not always stated, and the groups’ own claims are not independently verified. A December 2025 joint advisory from CISA, the FBI, NSA and partners listed water and wastewater among the sectors affected and described the attacks as opportunistic and the groups as lacking sophisticated capability, yet said they have damaged vulnerable infrastructure, mainly through poorly secured VNC connections to OT devices. These cases are historical; no new attack on a water system has been reported in the past 30 days. It leads this edition because it documents physical damage at water utilities from low-skill tampering that basic exposure and password controls would block (editorial assessment). - Bloomberg News, 27 Oct 2026 (partly paywalled; summary by Meduza, 28 Oct 2026); Denmark’s Defence Intelligence Service attribution, reported by Euronews, 19 Dec 2025; CISA, FBI, NSA and partners joint advisory, 9 Dec 2025 (NSA release) - Review published 27 Oct 2026; Danish attack Dec 2024, attributed Dec 2025; Texas case 2024

item.title: [High] Supermarket refrigeration attacks have spread: after about 700 French stores in October, a new wave hit stores in five more European countries on 1–2 Nov
item.category: Incident — Cross-sector OT attacks on remotely managed controllers (food retail: France in Oct, five more European countries 1–2 Nov); confirmed by French authorities and retailers
item.description: Over the nights of 11–13 October, attackers remotely changed settings on web-managed refrigeration controllers in French supermarkets, forcing long or continuous defrost cycles that delayed alarms and pushed some cases to around 50 °C. Finance Minister Roland Lescure told Parliament on 13 October that about 700 stores were hit, at chains including Carrefour, Coopérative U, E.Leclerc, Intermarché/Netto and Monoprix; the Paris prosecutor has reported fires, and its cybercrime section has opened an inquiry. CERT-FR’s alert named Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controllers on 12 October, added Copeland and Dixell xweb units on 13 October, and says in its 16 October update that the campaigns are probably still ongoing; no new attack nights have been reported in France since 13 October, and the alert was still at that third version when re-checked on 2 November. On the night of 1–2 November a new wave hit supermarkets in Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, Ireland and Estonia: Ahold Delhaize reported an “IT incident” affecting refrigeration at dozens of Delhaize stores, Colruyt said five franchised Spar shops were attacked, the contractor that runs Delhaize’s refrigeration said evaporators had been switched into defrost, ICA, Coop and Musgrave (SuperValu) reported affected stores, and in Estonia refrigeration supplier Kitman Coldtech said an older Danfoss controller was set to 50°C; no actor has been named and no authority has linked the wave to France. No group has claimed it, no ransom was demanded and the entry route has not been established; Danfoss says most affected units are end-of-life. Les Mousquetaires, which runs Intermarché and Netto, has said the intrusion came through a company that maintained refrigeration at some of its stores; that is the retailer’s statement, not an official finding. Separately, Reuters reported on 29 October, citing four unnamed officials, that US Army and Air Force investigators, since joined by US Cyber Command, are treating freezer failures at at least six US military commissaries since late August as a suspected cyberattack, and that investigators have spoken to French police; no cause has been confirmed and no link to the French attacks established. No water system is involved. In our assessment the method, remote setpoint changes on controllers left reachable from the internet, mirrors this year’s attacks on US water systems, and Nozomi’s 13 October analysis ties the same exposed-access weakness to them. - CERT-FR alert CERTFR-2026-ALE-012, 12 Oct 2026, updated 13 and 16 Oct 2026 (primary); Finance Minister’s figure via AP, 13 Oct 2026; SecurityWeek, 15 Oct 2026; Les Mousquetaires statement via Dark Reading; Nozomi Networks analysis, 13 Oct 2026; Reuters, 29 Oct 2026, via The Next Web (US commissary investigation); Reuters, CBS News/AFP, RTÉ and ERR (2 Nov 2026) for the new wave - Attacks in France 11–13 Oct 2026; new wave in five more countries 1–2 Nov 2026; latest CERT-FR update 16 Oct 2026, still the current version on 2 Nov 2026; US investigation reported 29 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] Symantec: a China-nexus Warlock ransomware crew breached a water utility through on-premises SharePoint
item.category: Incident — Ransomware intrusion at a water utility (IT-side), vendor-reported
item.description: Symantec’s threat hunters reported on 1 October that a China-nexus threat actor it calls Longlegs (also tracked as Storm-2603) attacked at least four organizations in the past two months: a water utility, a telecom provider, a regional government body and a university, in Portuguese- and Spanish-speaking countries across Europe, Africa and Latin America. None is named. The group typically gets in by exploiting on-premises Microsoft SharePoint Server; the only CVEs Symantec names are the 2025 “ToolShell” flaws, plus related SharePoint bugs. It then uses a vulnerable signed driver to switch off security tools, a Visual Studio Code tunnel for persistence and the domain SYSVOL share to push ransomware. In Symantec’s detailed case study, an intrusion at an unnamed critical-infrastructure organization, Warlock reached at least 33 hosts; the report does not say whether that victim was the water utility, and it describes no OT or operational impact. In our assessment, a domain-wide ransomware push is exactly where a flat or over-trusted link between utility IT and SCADA turns an office outage into an operations problem. - Symantec / Carbon Black Threat Hunter Team report, 1 Oct 2026 (primary); BleepingComputer and SecurityWeek coverage - Intrusions over the previous two months; published 1 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] FBI and Secret Service: the FortiBleed campaign against Fortinet firewalls is still active, and their warning covers the water sector
item.category: Incident — Active credential-theft campaign against Fortinet firewalls and VPNs; FBI and Secret Service warning
item.description: In a joint advisory dated 6 October, the FBI and US Secret Service said the FortiBleed campaign against internet-facing FortiGate firewalls and SSL VPN gateways remains an active threat. There is no CVE: the attackers log in with reused or leaked credentials, crack passwords stored with legacy SHA-256 hashing and sniff authentication traffic. Once in, they create their own administrator accounts and sometimes reset or delete the originals, locking owners out, and the access is resold; the advisory says brokers have passed it to INC/Lynx and Payload ransomware affiliates, and SOCRadar says it has confirmed at least 12 ransomware deployments. The advisory covers all 16 US critical-infrastructure sectors and names water and wastewater among them; no water utility or control-system compromise has been described. SOCRadar’s count of 86,644 working device credentials in 194 countries dates from 19 June and is not a new figure. FortiGates often sit at a utility’s IT/OT boundary or carry vendor VPN access (editorial assessment). - FBI and US Secret Service joint advisory JCSA-20261006-01, 6 Oct 2026 (primary); The Hacker News and Cybersecurity Dive, 7 Oct 2026 - Advisory 6 Oct 2026; credential count dated 19 Jun 2026

item.title: [Low] Vicksburg, Mississippi ransomware takes city systems offline and disrupts utility bill payments
item.category: Incident — Municipal ransomware disrupts utility bill payments; no OT impact reported
item.description: Vicksburg Mayor Willis Thompson said in a statement on 1 October that a ransomware attack forced the city to take systems offline temporarily, disrupting its utility payment systems; emergency services were not affected. He said no one’s service will be cut off and no late-payment penalties will be charged while the investigation runs, and that the city is still working out whether personal or confidential information was compromised. The FBI, DHS, state officials and private responders are helping. No group has claimed the attack, and the city has not commented on any ransom demand. The reporting does not say which utility services the billing covers, and nothing points to water or wastewater control systems being affected. It is an IT-side incident, but municipal utilities that share city IT, billing and accounts should know what a city-wide shutdown would take down with it (editorial assessment). - Mayor’s statement, 1 Oct 2026, reported by The Record - Confirmed 1 Oct 2026

item.title: [Low] AVEVA says intruders accessed its corporate SharePoint, and that its software and production environments were not affected
item.category: Incident — Unauthorized access to an OT software vendor’s corporate document store; vendor says its software is not affected
item.description: AVEVA, whose HMI and SCADA software is common in water and wastewater plants (editorial assessment), posted security bulletin AVEVA-2026-007 by 23 October reporting unauthorized access to its corporate SharePoint, an internal document repository. The bulletin is headed to say it does not affect AVEVA software and platforms, and AVEVA says its software and production environments are separate and were not affected. It has activated its incident response plan, brought in outside cybersecurity experts and notified law enforcement, and says it will notify third parties if the investigation finds material impact on them. The entry is undated, does not say what documents were viewed or taken, names no attacker and recommends no customer action. Vendor document stores can hold project files, network drawings and support correspondence about customer sites (editorial assessment). - AVEVA security bulletin AVEVA-2026-007, undated, posted by 23 Oct 2026 (primary) - Posted by 23 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] Lumen: Volt Typhoon’s “Silent Train” network has reached targets since 2023 through hijacked routers and flaws in management platforms, and lists water among the sectors hit
item.category: Research — China-linked relay network and management-platform exploitation; water among the named sectors; no OT intrusion described
item.description: Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs reported on 28 October on Silent Train, a framework it attributes to Volt Typhoon, the group US agencies link to the Chinese state, and has seen in consistent use since November 2023. For each operation the operators build a single-use chain, from virtual private servers outside the US through hijacked home-office routers and IoT devices abroad and then in the US, sometimes in under two minutes, and take it apart afterwards, which makes the traffic hard to trace or block. The chains are used to reach targets and exploit IT and network management platforms: Lumen ties the group to flaws in Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN (CVE-2026-20127, CVSS v3.1 10.0, Cisco), VeloCloud Orchestrator (CVE-2026-16812), N-able N-central (CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876) and Versa Director, and likely an undisclosed Quest KACE flaw. Its key findings list water among the critical-infrastructure sectors affected, alongside energy, transportation, maritime, rail, aviation and emergency services; Lumen says it has notified hundreds of victims over three years, and Hawaii, California and Texas were the most targeted states. No victim is named and no intrusion into OT is described. These are different flaws from the VeloCloud and Cisco SD-WAN Manager bugs on other cards on this page. In our assessment, these platforms are what a utility’s IT or network provider uses to manage every site at once, so a compromise there reaches all of them. - Lumen Black Lotus Labs, 28 Oct 2026 (primary); Zero Day (Kim Zetter) and CyberScoop, 28 Oct 2026; KEV dates from CISA’s 30 Oct 2026 catalog - Activity since Nov 2023; report published 28 Oct 2026

item.title: [Medium] After France’s supermarket attacks, Forescout counts nearly 13,000 exposed refrigeration control services worldwide, and Waterfall sets out a minimum firewall checklist for small sites
item.category: Research — Internet exposure of remotely managed controllers after the French attacks; firewall guidance for small sites
item.description: Forescout’s Vedere Labs reported on 22 October that internet searches for ten refrigeration-controller product families returned 12,976 exposed service observations on 6,017 public IP addresses in 99 countries and territories; it counts services, not devices. About 80% of the Danfoss StoreView observations ran firmware older than 4.3.1, which carries known flaws, and Forescout counts more than 20 hacktivist claims of attacks on refrigeration systems since January, mostly in Spain and Italy (claims, not confirmed incidents). It says the entry route, actor and persistence in the French attacks are still unknown. Two days earlier, Waterfall Security’s Andrew Ginter, noting that the attacks look similar to recent ones on small US water utilities, set out a minimum setup for sites with little IT staff: a commercial-grade firewall with VPN, MFA and automatic updates; deny all traffic by default and allow only fixed addresses such as the service provider’s office, never home or mobile ones; back up and document the configuration; and replace the firewall about every four years. His theories about how the French attackers got in are his own and unconfirmed. - Forescout Vedere Labs, 22 Oct 2026 (primary); Waterfall Security, 20 Oct 2026; Industrial Cyber, 23 Oct 2026 - Published 20 and 22 Oct 2026

item.title: [Medium] MITRE ATT&CK v20 catalogues the July attacks on more than 30 Minnesota water utilities as campaign C0066
item.category: Research — MITRE ATT&CK v20 documents the 2026 US water-utility PLC campaign
item.description: MITRE’s ATT&CK v20, released this month, adds campaign C0066, “2026 U.S. Water Utilities Attacks” (entry created 8 October, last modified 13 October). It covers intrusions from 27 July at more than 30 municipal water and wastewater utilities in Minnesota, part of wider activity the FBI and EPA reported in at least seven states. The attackers reached internet-facing Rockwell/Allen-Bradley MicroLogix 1100 and 1400 PLCs through cellular gateways at water towers and sewer lift stations and changed their IP addresses and passwords to lock operators out. At least one victim’s program logic was altered, and reported effects included loss of water pressure, flooding and one treatment plant taken offline. MITRE says the campaign has not been formally attributed. The release also adds CyberAv3ngers’ IOControl malware, a Mexican campaign (C0064) that reached a municipal water utility, and a new ICS scripting technique, T1701. C0066’s technique list, from default credentials to modified parameters and program logic, is a ready-made checklist for detection and tabletop work. - MITRE ATT&CK campaign C0066, created 8 Oct 2026, modified 13 Oct 2026 (primary); Industrial Cyber, 16 Oct 2026 - Campaign activity from 27 Jul 2026; entry last modified 13 Oct 2026

item.title: [Critical] PHP2Shell: a suspected China-nexus actor chained the PHP flaws with a Linux kernel bug to take over about two dozen firewalls, and ABB now lists RTUs and wireless gateways, some with no fix
item.category: Advisory — Exploited PHP flaws in CISA KEV; confirmed root compromises of exposed Palo Alto firewalls; OT vendor products affected, some with no fix
item.description: Both PHP2Shell flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (each CVSS v4.0 9.2, PHP Group), have been in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog since 26 October. Research by Dream, verified by Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 on 29 October, found that a suspected China-nexus actor chained them with the Linux kernel flaw CVE-2026-46300 to gain root on about two dozen internet-exposed Palo Alto firewalls and management servers on 23–24 October, with victims in the US (including a US government-affiliated network), Japan, Taiwan and South Korea, and then stole Active Directory credentials. CISA added the kernel flaw, a local privilege escalation, to KEV on 28 October; it also sits in the Linux subsystem of Siemens SIMATIC S7-1500 CPU 1518(F)-4 PN/DP MFP controllers, fixed in V3.1.7 for V3.1.6, with no fix for V3.1.5. Palo Alto’s advisory, Critical since 27 October, reports exploitation of PAN-OS management interfaces exposed to the internet, and all PAN-OS hotfixes were out by 29 October. No OT operator has been named, and no exploitation of Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808 units, which run PAN-OS and are fixed through Siemens support, has been reported. OT vendors keep adding products. On 30 October ABB listed its Netcontrol RTUs and NAM, with no fix yet, and its Arctic ARG/ARP/ARR/ARC/ARM600 wireless gateways, which are obsolete and will not be fixed; on 29 October it listed ASPECT products, with no firmware fix at publication; and ABB had not published the planned APROL patch as of 31 October. Schneider Electric’s SESB-2026-295-01, now version 3.2.0 (30 October), keeps its EcoStruxure Control Engineering remediation and has added the Foxboro DCS H90 Server, with port blocking as the only mitigation. Siemens SSA-166980 (V1.2, 29 October) now lists affected energy products, including Spectrum Power grid-control software and AMIS TS, several without a fix. Rockwell still lists no affected products. WaterISAC updated its PHP2Shell notice on 29 October with CISA’s SIGMA detection rule. PHP itself was fixed on 21 October in 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. In our assessment, the firewall between business IT and SCADA remains the most exposed point for utilities, followed by billing and payment portals that outside providers run on PHP. - Palo Alto Networks advisory CVE-2026-109618, 21 Oct 2026, updated 29 Oct 2026 (primary); Unit 42, 29 Oct 2026; The Record, 29 Oct 2026; Cybersecurity Dive, 30 Oct 2026; CISA KEV (catalog of 30 Oct 2026); ABB advisories 2NGA003256 and 2NGA003224 (30 Oct 2026), ASPECT 9AKK108473A4963 (29 Oct 2026) and SA26P015 (23 Oct 2026); Schneider Electric SESB-2026-295-01 v3.2.0, 30 Oct 2026; Siemens SSA-166980 V1.2 (29 Oct 2026), SSA-566512 and SSA-019113; WaterISAC notice, updated 29 Oct 2026; Rockwell SD1802 - PHP fixes 21 Oct 2026; KEV 26 and 28 Oct 2026; firewall compromises 23–24 Oct 2026; latest vendor updates 30 Oct 2026

item.title: [Critical] Ivanti Connect Secure: CISA adds two more flaws from the chain that gave attackers root on patched VPNs; check Ivanti for the build that fixes the root escalation
item.category: Advisory — Exploited VPN flaw chain, three flaws now in CISA KEV; fix for the root escalation unconfirmed; remote-access edge
item.description: Ivanti disclosed on 13 October that attackers chained flaws to run commands as root on fully patched Connect Secure VPN appliances at a limited number of customers. CVE-2026-104935 (CVSS v3.1 8.6, Ivanti), an authentication bypass that leads to unauthenticated command execution, went into CISA’s KEV catalog the same day. On 30 October CISA added two more: CVE-2026-111357, a privilege escalation to root in Connect Secure (CVSS v3.1 7.0, MITRE as CNA; due 2 November), whose CVE record has existed since 15 October, and CVE-2026-118527 (due 13 November). CISA says both can be chained with CVE-2026-104935. This corrects our earlier statement that the privilege-escalation flaw had no CVE. NVD lists versions up to 22.8R2.5 and 25.1.x before 25.1.1.3 as affected by CVE-2026-111357, so a build that fixed CVE-2026-104935 may not close the whole chain; check Ivanti’s advisory for the build that fixes CVE-2026-111357. Volexity, which found the chain during an incident response, tracks the actor as a new group, UTA0576; Volexity and Defused date exploitation to at least early October (1–3 October). The intruders left no web shell; they stole domain credentials, queried Active Directory for LAPS passwords and BitLocker keys, sprayed passwords and wiped logs. CISA warns that Ivanti’s Integrity Checker may not detect the compromise. No water-sector victim has been reported; Connect Secure is a common front door for utility staff and vendor remote access (editorial assessment). - Ivanti advisory and Volexity report, 13 Oct 2026 (primary); CISA KEV additions 13 and 30 Oct 2026 (catalog of 30 Oct 2026); CVE-2026-111357 record and NVD configuration via the CIRCL vulnerability database; CyberScoop, SecurityWeek and Cybersecurity Dive coverage, 13–14 Oct 2026 - Exploited from early Oct 2026; KEV 13 Oct 2026; two more chain flaws added to KEV 30 Oct 2026

item.title: [Critical] Citrix NetScaler: a fourth critical flaw follows three exploited ones, and builds that fixed September’s zero-days need upgrading again
item.category: Advisory — Three exploited NetScaler flaws in CISA KEV and a fourth critical SAML flaw; remote-access edge
item.description: Citrix disclosed CVE-2026-107406 on 8 October (bulletin CTX697191), a memory overflow in NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances configured as a SAML service provider or identity provider, rated CVSS v4.0 9.5. Citrix says it may allow code execution or denial of service and knows of no exploitation; it was still not in KEV as of CISA’s 30 October catalog. Builds that fixed the late-September zero-days stay exposed when used as a SAML identity provider, and CISA urged customers to patch on 9 October. The earlier trio is exploited and in KEV: CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 (added 27 September) and CVE-2026-88779 (added 4 October), which Citrix and watchTowr describe as a crash bug and which CISA says attackers use to force reboots so that code planted through CVE-2026-88771 runs. Google’s threat intelligence group counts dozens of affected organizations and Arctic Wolf at least 78 targeted; Shadowserver saw more than 20,000 exposed instances in late September. WaterISAC alerted members on 28 September, and no water-sector victim has been reported. NetScaler often fronts VPN and vendor access into utility networks (editorial assessment). - Citrix bulletins CTX697174 and CTX697191 (8 Oct 2026); CISA KEV and CISA patch alert, 9 Oct 2026; GTIG, Arctic Wolf, watchTowr and Shadowserver via Cybersecurity Dive and SecurityWeek; WaterISAC notification, 28 Sep 2026 - KEV additions 27 Sep and 4 Oct 2026; fourth flaw disclosed 8 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] Cisco ASA and FTD firewalls: an exploited zero-day lets an unauthenticated attacker crash the remote-access VPN, and CISA’s deadline is 1 November
item.category: Advisory — Exploited zero-day in Cisco firewall remote-access VPN, CISA KEV; denial of service at the IT/OT boundary
item.description: Cisco disclosed CVE-2026-76418 on 28 October in advisory cisco-sa-asaftd-tunnel-dos-s6mgkb75 and says its PSIRT became aware of active exploitation this month. On Secure Firewall ASA and FTD software with the SSL remote-access VPN enabled and secondary authentication configured on a tunnel group, including the default group, a crafted request from an unauthenticated remote attacker makes the device reload; no successful VPN login is needed. Cisco rates it CVSS v3.1 8.6. It is a denial of service, not code execution, but each reload drops every VPN session through the firewall. There is no workaround: disabling secondary authentication mitigates it at the cost of weaker VPN logins, and Cisco recommends upgrading. CISA added it to KEV on 29 October with a 1 November federal deadline. Cisco names no attacker or victims, and no water-sector victim has been reported. Where an ASA or FTD carries operator, on-call or vendor access into treatment plants and pumping sites, repeated reloads would cut remote monitoring and support (editorial assessment). - Cisco advisory cisco-sa-asaftd-tunnel-dos-s6mgkb75, 28 Oct 2026 (primary); CISA KEV, 29 Oct 2026 (catalog of 30 Oct 2026); The Hacker News, 30 Oct 2026 - Disclosed 28 Oct 2026; KEV 29 Oct 2026, deadline 1 Nov 2026

item.title: [High] CISA lists the BeyondTrust Remote Support zero-day as exploited; a suspected China-nexus espionage group has used it since late August
item.category: Advisory — Exploited zero-day in a remote-support appliance, CISA KEV; suspected state-linked espionage; no water victim reported
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-102764 in BeyondTrust Remote Support to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 16 October; the 19 October federal deadline has passed. A day before the listing, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) reported that a suspected China-nexus espionage group it tracks as ARMORY CASTLE (formerly UNC5221) had exploited the flaw, rated CVSS v4.0 9.3 by its CNA, as a zero-day since late August. The intruders gained root on Remote Support appliances, harvested credentials, deleted logs and used the tool’s file transfer to take documents. BeyondTrust shipped a fix on 8 October; self-hosted appliances without automatic updates must be patched by hand. GTIG names no victims or sectors, no water utility has reported a compromise, and we found no new victim or attribution reporting since mid-October. In our assessment, remote-support tools are a common way integrators and SCADA vendors reach utility workstations. - CISA KEV, 16 Oct 2026 (catalog of 30 Oct 2026); Google Threat Intelligence Group, 15 Oct 2026 (primary); BeyondTrust advisory BT26-05; SecurityWeek, 16 Oct 2026 - Exploitation from late Aug 2026; fix 8 Oct 2026; disclosed 15 Oct 2026; KEV 16 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator: an exploited flaw that lets any logged-in user take operator control is now in CISA KEV
item.category: Advisory — Exploited flaw in an SD-WAN management console, CISA KEV; remote-site connectivity
item.description: Arista disclosed CVE-2026-114625 on 22 October in Security Advisory 0199 and says it is known to be actively exploited. The SQL-injection flaw in on-premises VeloCloud Orchestrator (VCO), the management console for VeloCloud SD-WAN, lets any authenticated user, down to the Enterprise Read Only role, impersonate a built-in superuser operator account and reach internal-only functions, putting the orchestrator and the data it manages at risk. Arista rates it CVSS v3.1 9.9 / v4.0 9.4. Releases 5.2.3.18, 6.1.3.10 and 6.4.2.12 fix it; hosted and dedicated orchestrators have already been patched, and end-of-support versions were not assessed. Arista lists two attacker IP addresses but names no actor or victims. CISA added the flaw to KEV on 23 October with a 26 October federal deadline, now passed. No water-sector victim has been reported. In our assessment, an SD-WAN orchestrator controls the links between a utility’s offices, treatment plants and remote sites, so a takeover reaches every site it manages. - Arista Security Advisory 0199, 22 Oct 2026 (primary); CISA KEV, 23 Oct 2026 (catalog of 30 Oct 2026) - Disclosed 22 Oct 2026; KEV 23 Oct 2026, deadline 26 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] Siemens Software Center: attackers abuse a DLL-loading flaw in a ClickFix malware campaign, and CISA adds it to KEV
item.category: Advisory — Exploited flaw in a Siemens Windows application, CISA KEV; abused in a ClickFix malware campaign
item.description: Siemens confirmed on 19 October that CVE-2026-110936, an uncontrolled search-path flaw in its Siemens Software Center Windows application, is being exploited. Attackers bundle a genuine, validly signed copy of the program with their own DLLs, so the trusted Siemens binary loads their code; Siemens ties the activity to the “Romulus” ClickFix campaign, which lures users into running the files themselves, and says no Siemens system, product or update channel was breached to its knowledge. It names no final malware. Siemens rates the flaw CVSS v3.1 6.7 / v4.0 8.4 and fixed it in V4.0.9.8; existing installations update automatically on next start. CISA added it to KEV on 20 October with a 3 November federal deadline and republished the advisory as ICSA-26-295-03 on 22 October. In our assessment, the risk for utilities sits on engineering and SCADA workstations: application-allowlisting rules that trust anything Siemens-signed would let such a bundle run. - Siemens ProductCERT exploitation notice, 19 Oct 2026, and SSA-580366 (primary); CISA KEV, 20 Oct 2026; CISA ICSA-26-295-03, 22 Oct 2026; SecurityWeek, 19 Oct 2026 - Advisory 15 Oct 2026; exploitation confirmed 19 Oct; KEV 20 Oct; CISA republication 22 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] A FortiManager breach at a managed service provider exposed settings for 500-plus client firewalls; the FortiOS flaw used to gain root is now in KEV
item.category: Advisory — Exploited FortiOS flaw in CISA KEV; FortiManager-to-FortiGate compromise at a managed service provider
item.description: Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 reported on 14 October that attackers broke into a telecommunications managed service provider through its FortiManager, using the 2024 “FortiJump” flaw CVE-2024-47575, then used CVE-2025-61624, a FortiOS command-line path-traversal flaw, to get root on managed FortiGate firewalls and plant a loader Unit 42 calls PEERSTITCH. The stolen archive held configuration data for more than 500 FortiGates protecting the provider and its clients; Unit 42 calls that exposure of configuration and credential material, not confirmed intrusion into the client networks. It tracks the cluster as CL-STA-0954 (also UNC5820) and names no state. Fortinet fixed CVE-2025-61624 in April, rates it Medium and says it needs privileged, authenticated access; CISA added it to KEV on 16 October with a 19 October deadline. The CVE record lists Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808, which can run FortiOS, among affected products. Many small utilities have their firewalls managed by an outside provider (editorial assessment). - Unit 42 report, 14 Oct 2026 (primary); Fortinet PSIRT FG-IR-26-122; CISA KEV, 16 Oct 2026; The Hacker News, 16 Oct 2026 - Flaw fixed Apr 2026; report 14 Oct 2026; KEV 16 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] FortiMail and Cisco SD-WAN Manager zero-days join CISA’s exploited list; Fortinet now lists fixed releases
item.category: Advisory — Two more exploited edge zero-days in CISA KEV: FortiMail and Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager
item.description: Two more internet-facing products were confirmed exploited at the turn of the month. Fortinet advisory FG-IR-26-175, published 1 October, covers CVE-2026-104286 (CVSS 9.8), a path-traversal flaw in the web interface of FortiMail’s identity-based encryption feature that lets an unauthenticated attacker write arbitrary files on the system. Fortinet says it has been reported exploited in the wild, and CISA added it to KEV on 1 October with a 4 October deadline. Fortinet’s 5 October update lists fixed releases 7.4.9, 7.6.7 and 8.0.2; the 7.2 branch must move to 7.4 or later. Cisco disclosed on 30 September that CVE-2026-76504 (CVSS 9.8) in Catalyst SD-WAN Manager lets a remote attacker bypass an authentication rule on an API endpoint and gain administrator access; Cisco says it saw active exploitation in September, CISA listed it the same day with a 3 October deadline, and Cisco revised its advisory on 2 October. Neither vendor has named an actor or victims. In our assessment, FortiMail sits in the corporate mail path that utility staff and vendors rely on, and an SD-WAN manager can control the links to treatment plants and remote pumping sites. - Fortinet PSIRT FG-IR-26-175, 1 Oct 2026, updated 5 Oct 2026; Cisco advisory cisco-sa-sdwan-webauth-xr8beuuU, 30 Sep 2026, revised 2 Oct 2026; CISA KEV - KEV additions 30 Sep and 1 Oct 2026; Fortinet fixed releases listed 5 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] CISA republishes Mitsubishi Electric’s ICONICS advisory: fixes for GENESIS64 and GENESIS, none for MC Works64, GENESIS32 or BizViz
item.category: Advisory — Critical-rated flaws in ICONICS SCADA, HMI and historian software, now republished by CISA; no fix for three older products
item.description: CISA republished Mitsubishi Electric advisory 2026-006 as ICSA-26-300-02 on 27 October, twelve days after the vendor released it. It covers flaws across Mitsubishi’s ICONICS SCADA, HMI and historian products. The highest-rated, CVE-2026-16438 (CVSS v3.1 9.1 in Mitsubishi’s advisory), gives the administrator account default DCOM permissions. CVE-2026-16436 (v3.1 8.1) is a shared, fixed challenge-response that can unlock any user account once an attacker obtains the response; the advisory also lists a second challenge-response flaw, CVE-2026-16437 (v3.1 6.4), and the older libwebp bug CVE-2023-4863 (v3.1 8.2). Affected are GENESIS up to 11.03 and GENESIS64, ICONICS Suite, Hyper Historian, AnalytiX, MobileHMI and IoTWorX up to 10.97.3; version 10.98 and GENESIS 11.04 fix them (10.97.3 for libwebp). MC Works64, GENESIS32 and BizViz, all versions, will get no fix, and Mitsubishi advises replacing them with GENESIS64 or GENESIS. None of the ICONICS-specific flaws is in KEV; the bundled libwebp flaw CVE-2023-4863 has been in KEV since 13 September 2023 from browser exploitation. No exploitation of ICONICS products is reported. CISA’s republication lists only Critical Manufacturing as the sector, but GENESIS64 also runs SCADA and HMI screens in water and wastewater (editorial assessment). - Mitsubishi Electric PSIRT advisory 2026-006, 15 Oct 2026 (primary); CISA ICSA-26-300-02, 27 Oct 2026, via the CIRCL vulnerability database; CIRCL record for CVE-2023-4863 (KEV entry) - Vendor advisory 15 Oct 2026; CISA republication 27 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] CISA flags WAGO controller and Moxa edge-gateway flaws, both listing water and wastewater: a low-privilege command injection to root and a hard-coded key
item.category: Advisory — CISA ICS advisories for controller and edge-gateway firmware; Water and Wastewater listed; no known exploitation
item.description: CISA’s 20 October batch includes two advisories that name Water and Wastewater Systems among the affected sectors. ICSA-26-293-02 republishes CERT@VDE’s VDE-2026-096 for WAGO CC100, PFC100 G2, PFC200 G2, TP600, Edge Controller and WP400 devices on firmware older than 4.10.0 (FW32). CVE-2026-80466 (CVSS v3.1 8.8) lets a logged-in, low-privileged user inject operating-system commands through routing settings in the web-based management interface, which a root helper then runs; CVE-2026-88850 (v3.1 8.1) lets low-privileged users change root-owned PROFIBUS settings. Firmware 4.10.0 (FW32) fixes both. ICSA-26-293-03 covers Moxa AIG-302 ThingsPro Edge gateways up to firmware 1.4.0: CVE-2026-109813, a hard-coded cryptographic key (v3.1 8.1 / v4.0 8.6), and a missing-authorization flaw, CVE-2026-109812 (v3.1 6.8 / v4.0 6.9); version 1.4.1 fixes both. Neither advisory reports exploitation, and neither is in KEV. Controllers and gateways like these often sit in pump-station and telemetry panels (editorial assessment). - CISA ICSA-26-293-02 (WAGO, republishing CERT@VDE VDE-2026-096) and ICSA-26-293-03 (Moxa, MPSA-262560), 20 Oct 2026, via the CIRCL vulnerability database (primary) - Published 20 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] October OT patches: Siemens S7-1500 web-server flaws have no fix yet; Schneider Sage RTUs and Ignition get updates
item.category: Advisory — October OT patch cycle: Siemens S7-1500, Schneider Sage RTU, Inductive Automation Ignition; no known exploitation
item.description: Siemens’ 13 October release includes SSA-591731, eight web-server flaws in S7-1500, ET 200SP, ET 200pro and Drive Controller CPUs, rated up to CVSS v3.1 9.6 (v4.0 9.4), that could let an attacker run code in a logged-in user’s browser and carry out PLC operations with that user’s rights. All versions are affected and only mitigations are available so far. A separate advisory, SSA-784472, lists 377 flaws in the optional Linux subsystem of the S7-1500 TM MFP module, also without a fix. Schneider Electric’s SEVD-2026-286-02 covers Sage RTUs (1410, 1430, 1450, 2400, 3030 Magnum and 4400) that do not properly verify firmware, so a modified image could be loaded when an administrator runs an update (CVE-2026-102250, CVSS v3.1 7.2 / v4.0 8.6); firmware C3414-500-S02L0 fixes it. CISA also flagged an Ignition SCADA privilege-escalation flaw, CVE-2026-92817 (CVSS v3.1 8.8), fixed in 8.1.55 and 8.3.9. CISA republished Siemens’ 13 October advisories on 22 October (ICSA-26-295-02 to -18), and the S7 web-server and TM MFP issues still had no fix. None is known to be exploited or listed in KEV. S7-1500 PLCs, Sage RTUs and Ignition all turn up in water and wastewater SCADA (editorial assessment). - Siemens ProductCERT SSA-591731 and SSA-784472; Schneider Electric SEVD-2026-286-02; CISA ICSA-26-286-01 (Ignition), all 13 Oct 2026 (primary); SecurityWeek ICS Patch Tuesday roundup, 14 Oct 2026; CISA republications ICSA-26-295-02 to -18, 22 Oct 2026 - Published 13 Oct 2026; CISA republished 22 Oct 2026

item.title: [Medium] WaterISAC: Fortinet has shipped fixes for FortiOS, FortiManager, FortiAnalyzer, FortiMail and FortiAuthenticator, with flaw details held until 10 November
item.category: Advisory — WaterISAC notice of Fortinet fixes released before the flaws are disclosed; no known exploitation
item.description: WaterISAC told members in a TLP:CLEAR notification on 27 October that Fortinet has released coordinated security fixes for FortiOS, FortiManager, FortiAnalyzer, FortiMail and FortiAuthenticator, and that CVE IDs, CVSS scores and technical details are due in Fortinet’s PSIRT advisories on 10 November. WaterISAC says no active exploitation has been reported so far, but warns that attackers can study the fixes to build exploits before then, and that vulnerability scanners will not flag affected devices until CVE data exists, so versions must be checked directly. The fixed releases it lists are FortiOS 8.0.2, 7.6.8, 7.4.13 and 7.2.14; FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer 8.0.2, 7.6.8, 7.4.12 and 7.2.13; FortiMail 8.0.2, 7.6.7 and 7.4.9 (7.2 users should move to 7.4 or later); and FortiAuthenticator 8.0.4 and 6.6.11. FortiSASE has been updated automatically, and FortiManager Cloud may need a manual update. Fortinet’s chief information security officer described the release in a 21 October blog post, saying it includes critical and high-severity fixes that came out of Fortinet’s AI-assisted security testing and urging customers to start with internet-facing devices; this corrects our earlier note that we had not seen a public Fortinet notice. FortiGate firewalls often sit at a utility’s IT/OT boundary or carry vendor VPN access (editorial assessment). - WaterISAC TLP:CLEAR vulnerability notification, 27 Oct 2026; Fortinet blog, Carl Windsor, 21 Oct 2026 (primary) - Fortinet blog 21 Oct 2026; WaterISAC notification 27 Oct 2026; Fortinet advisories and CVE details due 10 Nov 2026

item.title: [Medium] Moxa: its remote-access client can be fooled by a fake server, and an end-of-life OnCell cellular gateway has flaws that will not be fixed
item.category: Advisory — Remote-access client and end-of-life cellular gateway flaws; no fix for the gateway; no known exploitation
item.description: Moxa advisory MPSA-269510, published 27 October, covers three flaws. In the Moxa Remote Connect (MRC) Client, an OpenVPN-based remote-access tool, CVE-2026-111459 (CVSS v4.0 7.6, scored by Moxa) means the client accepts a configuration from the server without properly validating the server’s certificate, so an attacker on the network path could pose as the MRC server; versions 1.0.0 to 4.2.0 are affected, and 4.2.2, available through Moxa support, fixes it. The OnCell G3150A-LTE cellular gateway ships static HTTPS and CA private keys in its firmware (CVE-2026-111460, v4.0 7.7) and has a command-injection flaw in its SMS upgrade feature, reachable by a privileged attacker when SMS management is enabled (CVE-2026-111461, v4.0 7.5). The gateway is end-of-life, so neither will be fixed; the mitigations are to reset the device so it generates new keys and to keep SMS management disabled, as it is by default. No exploitation has been reported and none of the three is in KEV. Cellular gateways connect lift stations, tanks and wells to SCADA, and integrators use remote-connect clients to reach them (editorial assessment). - Moxa security advisory MPSA-269510, 27 Oct 2026 (primary); CVE records via the CIRCL vulnerability database; CERT-FR CERTFR-2026-AVI-1393 - Published 27 Oct 2026

item.title: [Medium] CISA flags open-source code inside OT products: an lwIP SMTP-client overflow rated 9.8 and six Eclipse Milo OPC UA flaws
item.category: Advisory — Flaws in two open-source components used inside OT products; CISA lists water and wastewater
item.description: Two CISA advisories this month name Water and Wastewater Systems among the affected sectors for flaws in widely reused open-source code. ICSA-26-279-02 (6 October) covers CVE-2026-15340, a buffer overflow in the SMTP client of the lwIP embedded TCP/IP stack, version 2.2.1, rated CVSS v3.1 9.8; it is fixed by an upstream patch rather than a new release, and real-world exposure depends on whether a device maker uses lwIP’s SMTP client at all. ICSA-26-288-01 (15 October) covers six flaws in Eclipse Milo, a Java OPC UA client and server library, the highest rated CVSS v3.1 8.2; version 1.1.5 fixes them, and the older 0.6.x line will get no fix. Neither is in KEV, and no exploitation has been reported. The practical exposure sits in the products that embed these components, which makes this a question for your SCADA, telemetry and instrument vendors (editorial assessment). - CISA ICSA-26-279-02, 6 Oct 2026, and ICSA-26-288-01, 15 Oct 2026, via the CIRCL vulnerability database (primary) - Published 6 and 15 Oct 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA’s new four-year strategy, “CISA 2030”, names operational technology security as a priority and starts a review of the agency’s core services
item.category: Regulation & Policy — CISA four-year strategy; no new obligations
item.description: CISA released “CISA 2030: Defend, Harden, Prevail” on 26 October. Its three pillars cover day-to-day defense, longer-term hardening and resilience to disruption, and the plan commits the agency to put its resources where they will have the greatest impact, including assessing which infrastructure matters most through a national risk register and studying how assets depend on one another. Under the Defend pillar CISA says it will help operators improve OT security, with asset visibility and intrusion detection named, and it gives supply-chain security particular attention. The agency will begin reviewing its core services and capabilities within 60 days, finish an implementation plan with success metrics within 180 days and report on progress after a year. Acting Director Nick Andersen describes a shift to a more “anticipatory” stance. The strategy creates no new requirements for utilities, and water and wastewater are not singled out in the coverage we reviewed. Utilities that use CISA’s free assessments, scanning or regional advisors should watch the outcome of the services review (editorial assessment). - CISA 2030 strategy, 26 Oct 2026; Cybersecurity Dive and CyberScoop, 26 Oct 2026; Help Net Security, 27 Oct 2026 - Released 26 Oct 2026; services review due to start within 60 days

item.title: [Info] EPA will run a free webinar on 18 November on designing tabletop exercises for drinking water and wastewater utilities
item.category: Regulation & Policy — Free EPA preparedness webinar for drinking water and wastewater utilities
item.description: WaterISAC posted on 22 October that EPA will host a free one-hour webinar on 18 November, 1–2 p.m. ET, on building a tabletop exercise with EPA’s TTX Tool for drinking water and wastewater utilities (ttx.epa.gov). EPA will explain why tabletop exercises are worth the time, an exercise designer who has used the tool will share lessons, and a utility that recently took part in one will describe the experience; attendees are invited to bring questions. WaterISAC’s post does not include a registration link, so watch EPA’s water-security pages and WaterISAC channels for sign-up details. In our assessment, MITRE’s C0066 entry for this summer’s attacks on Minnesota water utilities gives a ready-made scenario for a first exercise. - WaterISAC TLP:CLEAR posting relaying EPA, 22 Oct 2026; EPA TTX Tool (ttx.epa.gov) - Posted 22 Oct 2026; webinar 18 Nov 2026

item.title: [Info] Accenture, Dragos and SANS launch a foundation offering free OT monitoring, deployment and training to up to 500 small utilities, water and wastewater included
item.category: Regulation & Policy — Industry-funded OT security programme for small utilities
item.description: Accenture, Dragos and the SANS Institute announced the Community Cyber Resilience Foundation on 20 October: a nonprofit with about $10 million in initial funding and services, with technology support from Elastic. Its first phase covers up to 500 utilities with annual revenue under $100 million, a threshold the companies say covers 97% of utilities, on top of the more than 100 already in Dragos’s Community Defense Program. The foundation’s site lists water, wastewater, electric and natural-gas utilities in the US and Canada; Dragos’s announcement refers to US utilities. Members get the Dragos Platform, Neighborhood Keeper and OT-CERT; assessment, deployment and ongoing support from Accenture; SANS training with GIAC certification; and hardware funding where needed. Enrollment “opens soon” and an interest list is open now. There is no government involvement. In our assessment, this removes the cost barrier for small systems that have never had OT network monitoring; finding staff time to act on it is the harder part. - Dragos announcement, 20 Oct 2026 (primary); Community Cyber Resilience Foundation website; The Record and Industrial Cyber, 21 Oct 2026 - Announced 20 Oct 2026; enrollment not yet open

item.title: [Info] CISA’s final cyber incident-reporting rule reaches White House review; text and start dates are not yet public
item.category: Regulation & Policy — Federal cyber incident-reporting rule (CIRCIA)
item.description: The White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs logged receipt of CISA’s final rule under the Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act (RIN 1670-AA04) on 1 October, and the review is pending. The statute set an October 2025 deadline, and CISA’s later targets of May and September 2026 slipped; HIPAA Journal reports publication is expected before year-end. The law calls for covered entities to report covered cyber incidents within 72 hours and ransom payments within 24 hours, but no obligation applies until the final rule sets its dates. The rule text, including which water and wastewater systems it covers, is not public, and the review can still change it. No publication of the final rule had been reported as of 31 October. - OIRA regulatory review record (reginfo.gov), received 1 Oct 2026 (primary); HIPAA Journal, 5 Oct 2026; Paubox, 8 and 14 Oct 2026 - Under review since 1 Oct 2026; no publication reported as of 31 Oct 2026
